_doc: The saloon's building spec (format: experiments/building_lab/FORMAT.md). Made from docs/concept/saloon-sheet.png (the look and the layout's ideas), Sean's saloon picture docs/concept/targets/10_saloon_interior.png (the look inside) and Sean's answers (docs/briefs/building-pipeline.md's critiques; 2026-10-21/22). Sizes come from this file, never off the pictures. Metres in the building's own space: x along the front from its west corner (0) to its east corner (15.24), z back from the front wall's outer stud face, y up from the ground; the front faces -Z (the street), as FalseFrontBuilding's. Feet in the notes because the town was laid out and framed in them.

identity.owner: Joe Doyle, who came out with the railroad's grading crews and stayed when they moved on
identity.trade: saloon, card room and lodging house (five rooms let by the night or the week)
identity.means: the richest man on Main Street after the bank; built it new on a double lot four years ago, the first two-storey frame in town
identity.age_and_repair: 4 years: the paint on the front still red, the sides never painted and already grey; the floor worn pale from the door to the bar; one gallery baluster replaced in raw pine
clues: a brass foot rail polished bright where boots rest, dull at the ends nobody stands
a faro layout chalked on the middle table, a cuspidor at every post
a sign over the back bar: NO CREDIT, NO GUNS ABOVE STAIRS
a spare key board behind the bar for the five rooms upstairs
a path worn through the yard grass to the outhouse

lot._doc: Sean, 2026-10-21/22: widen the lot (an important building: a double lot of 50 ft) and take the room from Freight Street, which moves east; nothing on the south side moves. town.json changes when this is used for real (FORMAT.md 'What using it for real needs'): Saloon stays at x 5, its SouthBoardwalk lengthens to 16.4, Freight Street's line moves from x 23 to 28.5 (its west edge from 17 to 22.5), RangeCover from x 30 to 35.5; the outside stair and the side balcony take x 20.24..21.66 in town.

levels._doc: The sheet's cutaway: 12 ft (3.66 m) floor to floor downstairs, 10 ft (3.05 m) up (the brief's 'usable starting number'). The ground floor is four steps up from the street, as today's saloon (town.json floor_top 0.78).

frame._doc: A balloon frame (Bell 1858; Woodward 1865): 2x4 studs at 16 in running sill to plate through both storeys, the upper joists on a 1x6 ribbon let into them. Sections are dressed sizes, metres [width, depth]. Every span is checked by checks.gd's sizing (the Wood Handbook's figures for the game's woods, a crowd's 40 lb/ft2 on the floors and 60 on the balcony, L/360).

tall._doc: The balloon studs run 7-10 m sill to plate, carrying the roof's trusses, the upper floor and the balcony: 3x4 (a 2x4 that long buckles under a crowd upstairs; checks.gd).

truss._doc: Queen-post trusses (Tredgold: the queen post for 30-45 ft spans; here 50 ft between the walls' outer faces, the tie in two lengths scarfed over the rooms' wall) at 10 ft, carrying purlins, common rafters and boards.

girders._doc: Lines under the ground floor's joists (the joists span 10 ft or less between them), each on stone piers; inside the cellar on its posts.

cellar._doc: Sean, 2026-10-21: yes, and big. Kegs and spirits kept cool under the bar and the kitchen (the west half); rubble-stone walls, stone flags, six posts under the girders, reached by a trap and a stair in the kitchen. The floor over it is on real joists, so a blast or a fire can drop it in. The trap runs girder to girder (no joist is cut short), its two leaves folded back on the floor; the stair under it steep, as a cellar's (8.3 in risers on 7.9 in treads), with 2.1 m of head room under the floor's edge.

posts._doc: The gallery's posts (8x8, chamfered: Sean's picture), floor to the beams, each on a pier. 'wall' posts stand in a wall's stud line under a beam's end.

walls._doc: The front: lap siding in the saloon's red to the false front's top; the tall door (6 by 9 ft) with batwings, four windows; upstairs two doors to the street balcony, three windows; the sign on the false front over the balcony.
The west wall stands against the store: no windows. The bar's back wall.
The east wall, to Freight Street: the stair inside runs up it; windows to the stores, the stairwell and the back bedroom; a door from the side balcony into the front gallery.
The hall's back wall: it carries the back rooms' joists over it. A door to the back room, one behind the bar to the kitchen.
Rooms 4 and 5 over the bar, on the beam at x 3.66: their doors open on the west gallery. No windows (the west wall stands against the store).

stairs._doc: Up the east wall from the hall to the back gallery (the sheet's plan and its view from the entrance): 19 risers of 7.6 in, 18 treads of 10 in (two risers and a tread 25 in, Blondel's rule as the period stairbuilders give it), 3 ft 4 in wide, its open side railed.
Sean, 2026-10-21: keep the sheet's outside stair (a second way up). Up the east wall from the yard to the side balcony (Freight Street side), rising toward the street.
Four steps from the yard to the kitchen's back door.

balconies._doc: Sean: both balconies. Over the street, 8 ft deep over the boardwalk, on 6x6 posts at 10 ft along its edge, its joists on a ledger through the siding into the front wall's studs, wrapping round the east corner to the outside stair's head. Its corner beyond the east wall and the side landing on a beam along x 16.34.

galleries._doc: Sean: the gallery looking down into the saloon (the sheet's 'open to bar below'). Rails at 1 m on the well's edges, oak (the picture's balustrade).

rooms.use: drinking, cards, the piano, the bar
the owner's stores and his desk
the cook; the trap to the cellar; the back door to the yard
the doors to the street balcony; a lookout over the hall
the stair's head; rooms 1 to 3's doors
a bedroom, no window: a cheap room lit by its lamp (Sean, 2026-10-22, issue #242)
a bedroom, no window: a cheap room lit by its lamp (Sean, 2026-10-22, issue #242)

fixtures._doc: The bar along the west wall under rooms 4 and 5, on your right as you walk in (Sean, 2026-10-22: as his picture and the sheet's view from the entrance), three 3 m sections, the customers to the east; the back bar against the wall behind, three 2.5 m sections. Kit parts, turned to face the room.

lamps._doc: Every lamp an OilLamp (a fitting: it falls with what holds it, smashes, spills burning oil). Sconces stand on a bracket member nailed to the wall's boards; table lamps on the card tables (they fall with the table, KitProp); the chandelier is a wheel of members hung from the truss on iron rods. A partition's sconces are on its - side unless `side` says +.

outbuildings._doc: Sean: an outhouse out back (no restrooms indoors in 1882). A two-holer, 5 by 4 ft, on sills, board and batten, a shed roof, its door to the house; 8 m from the back door.

use._doc: How the saloon is used, day in day out (docs/briefs/lived-in.md): the builder wears what each use touches, most where it's heaviest (the centre of a path, the middle of a tread, the rail where people stand), nothing where nobody goes. Daily counts are passings, climbs or uses a day; the marks grow with them and the years. A spot is where people stand (`feet`) at a rail (`at`). `edges`: the grime along the walls' feet and in the corners.

furniture._doc: The kit's tables take rings, elbows and knife cuts on their tops and scuffed boards round their chairs; the bar's foot rail is bright where the drinkers stand (their use points).

weather._doc: The front faces north on the street: mud splashed up its foot and the east side's (Freight Street's wagons); the back faces south and takes the sun: bleached, as the roof; water runs off each window's sill.

past.what: A fight over a pot at the middle table went up the stair and along the gallery: a man went into the rail and took a baluster with him; a ball fired at him is still in the post by the bar.
The stag hung over the back door for two years, then went to the back room: a pale patch and its nail holes.
A man bled out on the floor by the middle table; the patch was scrubbed, cleaner than the boards round it.
A bottle through the front window: one pane clearer than the rest.
M.K. cut into room 2's window frame, nearly painted over.
The eighth tread of the hall stair worked loose and was nailed down with a newer nail.
The spring flood took the back steps; they were rebuilt in new pine.
Kicked open with full hands so often its lower edge is chipped and the boards under its swing scuffed.
The outside stair's bottom tread split and was replaced.

materials._doc: Only woods the material lab approved (docs/PARTS.md 'Materials and look'): the interior woods Sean picked (C, 2026-10-21) inside the hall, the gallery and the rooms; the game's exterior woods outside; framing left as framing in the back rooms and the cellar.

sources: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material (FPL-GTR-282, 2021), ch. 5 (clear-wood strengths and stiffness) and ch. 7 (grades): the game's timber figures (config/timber.tres) and checks.gd's sizing.
William E. Bell, Carpentry Made Easy (Philadelphia, 1858; in print to 1904): the balloon frame, studs at 16 in sill to plate, the ribbon carrying the upper joists, girders on piers.
George E. Woodward, Woodward's Country Homes (1865): the balloon frame's practice in the West.

Thomas Tredgold, Elementary Principles of Carpentry (7th ed., rev. E. Wyndham Tarn, 1886): trusses, posts and beams, scarfed ties, its tables of scantlings. The queen post for spans of ~30-45 ft is the usual 19th-century rule; to check against the 1886 tables before production.

Fred T. Hodgson, The Carpenters' Steel Square and its Uses (1883): rafters, purlins and braces laid out. Stairs by the old rule (Blondel, Cours d'architecture, 1675-83) that two risers and a tread make about 25 in, as the period stairbuilders give it; a period stairbuilding manual to check before production.
Hand-built frontier saloons of the 1880s (the brief's reference set): the false front over a two-storey frame, the gallery round an open hall, rooms let upstairs, the outhouse in the yard.
